title: "Integral solvability and Blanchfield bordism for iterated infection"
- def-blanchfield-pairing-and-higher-order-rho-invariant
- lem-higher-order-blanchfield-pairings-are-nonsingular
locator: "§§4.1–4.3 and Appendix A, infection cobordism and Blanchfield bordism"

Let P be a winding-zero pattern satisfying the nonzero Blanchfield self-pairing hypothesis of Cha–Kim, and let K be an arbitrary knot. The iterated infection cobordism used in the proof of Cha–Kim Theorems A and B is an integral (n+1/2)-solution for the coefficient system specified there; its higher-order Blanchfield pairing is nonsingular and its metabolizer is represented by the infection curves.
[F2] The higher-order Blanchfield form is induced by Bockstein and Poincaré duality ([[def-blanchfield-pairing-and-higher-order-rho-invariant]]).
[F3] The relevant Blanchfield form is nonsingular when the coefficient homology vanishes ([[lem-higher-order-blanchfield-pairings-are-nonsingular]]).

2.1 To conclude integral (n+1/2)-solvability, one must verify that every dual class pairs as δ_ij, all Lagrangian self-pairings vanish, and each Lagrangian class lifts one derived stage further. The source’s handle and Blanchfield computations supply these checks, but they are not reproduced in steps 1.1–1.2. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2]

A full chain-level and intersection-form calculation is required. The inspected Cha–Kim argument supplies it but cites noncommutative Blanchfield nonsingularity and PTFA Ore localization, both unresolved local prerequisites.

Let P⊂S¹×D² be a winding-zero pattern. Assume the axis has nonzero classical Blanchfield self-pairing in the Alexander module of P(U), with the convention that the axis defines the class paired with itself. For either the locally flat topological concordance group C_top or the smooth concordance group C_sm, let Pⁿ be the n-fold composition of the induced satellite set map, with P⁰ the identity. For every n≥0, the quotient ⟨Pⁿ(C)⟩/⟨Pⁿ⁺¹(C)⟩ has infinite rank, where ⟨S⟩ denotes the subgroup generated by S and rank means dim_Q(A⊗_Z Q) for an abelian group A. For n≥1, Pⁿ is not a group homomorphism under the same hypotheses. No pairwise-coprime Alexander-polynomial assumption is part of these Theorems A and B.
[[def-blanchfield-pairing-and-higher-order-rho-invariant|Classical Blanchfield self-pairing convention]]
[F1] The classical Blanchfield self-pairing is the specialization of the linking form defined on the Alexander module ([[def-blanchfield-pairing-and-higher-order-rho-invariant]]).

[F2] The iterated infection cobordisms have the integral solvability and Blanchfield-bordism properties required in the Cha–Kim argument ([[lem-cha-kim-integral-solvability-and-blanchfield-bordism]]).

Assume the winding-zero and nonzero axis Blanchfield self-pairing hypotheses of Cha–Kim. For each finite stage of their iterated-infection construction, the companion knots can be chosen so that the relevant higher-order rho contribution has a fixed sign and dominates the sum of all remaining terms, using a uniform Cheeger–Gromov bound and signature functions supported near selected Alexander roots. Pairwise-coprime Alexander hypotheses are used only for the separate Theorem C separation argument, not for Theorems A or B.
**Given:** The exact finite family of PTFA coefficient systems, the nonzero Blanchfield self-pairing condition, and the winding-zero pattern in Cha–Kim’s construction.

actual_body_occurrences.text: id: lem-higher-order-blanchfield-pairings-are-nonsingular
title: "Classical and localized PTFA Blanchfield nonsingularity criteria"
- def-blanchfield-pairing-and-higher-order-rho-invariant

Then $H_1(M;R)$ is an $R$-torsion module and the coefficient Bockstein, oriented duality and evaluation define its Blanchfield pairing with target $K/R$. This pairing is nonsingular provided that on each component at least one of the following holds: every right ideal of $R$ is principal; $H_0(M_j;R)=0$; or the image of $\phi|_{\pi_1(M_j)}$ is cyclic. The last condition includes the usual integral infinite-cyclic coefficient case $R=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, without asserting that this ring is a principal ideal domain. No choice principle is assumed.
[[def-blanchfield-pairing-and-higher-order-rho-invariant]]

[F1] The Blanchfield convention is the inverse coefficient Bockstein after oriented duality, followed by evaluation; its first argument is conjugate-linear and its second argument right-linear. [[def-blanchfield-pairing-and-higher-order-rho-invariant]]

The unrestricted implication over an unlocalized multivariable group ring is false. The explicit $T^3$ example with coefficient image $\mathbb Z^2$ has nonzero torsion first homology and zero dual; it is recorded separately in [[cex-ptfa-ore-localization-alone-does-not-give-blanchfield-nonsingularity]]. This example is contextual evidence for the necessary coefficient hypothesis, not a supplier in the proof.

actual_body_occurrences.text: id: thm-winding-zero-infection-preserves-classical-blanchfield-pairings
title: Winding-zero infection preserves the classical Blanchfield pairing
Consequently $T=i_{P(K)}^{-1}i_P$ is an isometry of their classical Blanchfield pairings:

5.1 For $x,y\in H_1(M(P);\Lambda)$, the classes $(x,-Tx)$ and $(y,-Ty)$ lie in the kernel of $H_1(N;\Lambda)\to H_1(E;\Lambda)$ by the definition of $T$. The orthogonal sum of the boundary linking forms on this kernel is zero by step 3.2. Reversing the orientation of a closed component negates its cap fundamental class, hence negates inverse-cap duality and the resulting Blanchfield form; its Bockstein and evaluation are unchanged. Bilinearity gives $B_{-M(P(K))}(-Tx,-Ty)=-B_{P(K)}(Tx,Ty)$. Thus kernel isotropy says precisely $B_P(x,y)-B_{P(K)}(Tx,Ty)=0$, proving the claimed isometry. This uses the actual Bockstein linking forms and does not assume any general nonsingularity theorem. [F3, step 4.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra]
